messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh Patel is a 68-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment after years of trying to organize his life around an experience he still struggled to name aloud. He is divorced and works for a non-profit, where much of his week is spent in shared offices, community meeting rooms, and neighborhood buildings where people come and go unpredictably. In the first sessions, what stood out was not only the severity of his distress but the way he circled around the assault itself, stopping, starting, then falling silent. He would say that he knew exactly what had happened to him, that he could see it with terrible clarity, but when he tried to put it into words his mind seemed to lock. He would lower his eyes, grip the arms of the chair, and say, “I can’t say it right. I know it, but I can’t say it.”

When he did describe the event, it came in fragments tied to sensation. He had been overpowered and raped in an enclosed indoor space. What remained with him most vividly were not coherent images so much as sounds and pain: the sound of another person entering and moving in the room, the sudden noise that told him someone was there, the auditory details of the assault itself, and the pain in his body during it. In the present, when the memory returned, he did not experience it as distant recollection. He sometimes heard in his head the same sounds he had heard during the attack, as if the scene were opening again around him. At those moments he also felt pain in the same parts of his body that had hurt during the rape. The combination left him shaken and ashamed. What frightened him was not only remembering but the sense that his body and mind still reacted as though the event were somehow still happening.

In the weeks and months afterward, Rajesh became intensely alert to the possibility of intrusion. At home, he found himself listening constantly for sounds that might mean someone was entering. A shift in the hallway, a door in the building, a heavy footstep, an unexpected knock, any loud or sudden noise could make his whole body tense. He was particularly sensitive to sounds he could not immediately identify. He described sitting in his apartment in the evening, television off, straining to hear whether anyone was outside his door. He slept lightly and startled hard if awakened by noise. Unexpected touch was especially difficult. If someone placed a hand on his shoulder without warning, he reacted with visible alarm, jerking away before he could think.

These patterns entered his workday as well. At the non-profit, Rajesh began choosing seats with deliberate care, always placing his back against a wall so he could see the room and the door. In staff meetings he arrived early so no one else would take the spot he considered safest. If he had to meet with community members in unfamiliar offices, he scanned the layout immediately and positioned himself where nobody could come up behind him. Colleagues noticed that he seemed tense when people moved around him, especially in crowded rooms or when someone approached quietly from the side. He did not explain why. He had come to believe that his reactions showed he was a lousy coper, that other people would have found a way to move on, while he was still arranging chairs and doorways like a frightened man.

Being alone became another unbearable problem. He dreaded being alone in a room or building, especially if it was too quiet. If he stayed late at work and everyone else had gone, he felt exposed and unable to settle, listening for entry sounds until he finally left tasks unfinished. At home he tried to keep some form of contact or background presence around him rather than sit by himself with the silence. When feelings swelled beyond what he could bear, he sometimes hurt himself physically to release them. He described these moments not as wanting to die but as wanting the pressure inside him to break for a second into something simpler and more containable.

Over time, Rajesh’s view of himself hardened. He told himself that these reactions meant something fundamental had changed in him. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, as though the range of ordinary human feeling had narrowed into vigilance, shame, and brief, blunted stretches in between. He also felt permanently set apart from other people. Even in the community-centered mission of his job, he experienced himself as an outsider looking in, someone who could perform concern and connection without truly sharing in them.

What finally brought him to seek help was a recent accumulation of strain rather than a single new crisis. He had become exhausted by shaping every room for safety, by the shock of unexpected touch, by evenings spent listening for someone entering, and by his inability to speak plainly about what had happened to him. He said he was tired of living as if every sound carried a warning. At the same time, he was afraid that treatment would force him into words he still could not find, or prove that he was as damaged as he feared. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not dramatic relief but the possibility that he might one day sit in a room by himself, hear an ordinary noise, and remain in the present.
